subgroups.name: Figurative

subgroups.name: Symbolic

subgroups.name: Metafictional

techniques.name: Visual Imagery
techniques.definition: Language appealing to the sense of sight
techniques.effect: Helps reader visualize scenes and characters
techniques.example: The scarlet dress hung like a flag in the wind

techniques.name: Auditory Imagery
techniques.definition: Language that evokes sounds
techniques.effect: Intensifies emotional or sensory impact through sound
techniques.example: The whisper of leaves in autumn wind

techniques.name: Olfactory Imagery
techniques.definition: Language describing smells
techniques.effect: Triggers strong emotional and memory responses
techniques.example: The acrid smell of smoke filled the room

techniques.name: Gustatory Imagery
techniques.definition: Language describing taste
techniques.effect: Creates intimate, visceral sensory experience
techniques.example: The bitter pill of truth dissolved on his tongue

techniques.name: Tactile Imagery
techniques.definition: Language describing texture and physical sensation
techniques.effect: Engages reader through sense of touch
techniques.example: The rough bark scraped her palms raw

techniques.name: Kinaesthetic Imagery
techniques.definition: Language describing movement and physical sensation
techniques.effect: Conveys bodily experience and motion
techniques.example: Her limbs grew heavy; she sank into the chair

techniques.name: Synaesthesia
techniques.definition: Mixing sensory perceptions (e.g., hearing colors)
techniques.effect: Creates striking, surreal effects and fresh perspectives
techniques.example: The music was deep blue and resonant

techniques.name: Pathetic Fallacy
techniques.definition: Attributing human emotions to nature or objects
techniques.effect: Reflects character's inner state through external world
techniques.example: The grey sky wept as she left

techniques.name: Ekphrasis
techniques.definition: Detailed, vivid description of a visual artwork or scene
techniques.effect: Creates intensity and draws reader into moment
techniques.example: The marble statue's eyes seemed to follow her
techniques.etymology: Greek: ek- (out) + phrazein (to tell) — vivid description of a visual artwork

techniques.name: Sensory Accumulation
techniques.definition: Layering multiple sensory details in close proximity
techniques.effect: Overwhelms reader with immersive sensory experience
techniques.example: The hot sand, sharp cry of gulls, salt spray, blinding sun

techniques.name: Hypotyposis
techniques.definition: A strikingly vivid description of a scene or event, designed to create the impression that it is occurring before the reader's eyes in real time.
techniques.effect: Generates immediate, visceral engagement; collapses narrative distance so that the reader witnesses rather than reads, producing emotional and sensory immediacy.
techniques.example: Homer's battle descriptions in the Iliad, where violence is rendered with such physical precision it seems to unfold in the present moment.
techniques.etymology: From Greek hypotyposis, meaning 'sketch', 'outline' or 'vivid impression'.

techniques.name: Enargia
techniques.definition: Vivid, detailed description that renders a scene or object so clearly it seems to exist before the reader's eyes.
techniques.effect: Creates sensory immediacy and immersion; collapses the distance between reader and text so that description functions almost as presence.
techniques.example: Keats's 'To Autumn' describing the season's sights and textures with near-tactile vividness across every stanza.
techniques.etymology: From Greek enargeia, meaning 'vividness' or 'brilliance'.

techniques.name: Organic Imagery
techniques.definition: Imagery that conveys internal physical sensations such as hunger, fatigue, fear or nausea.
techniques.effect: Grounds emotion in visceral bodily experience.
techniques.example: a hollow ache spread through her chest
techniques.etymology: organic from Greek organikos, relating to an organ or instrument.

techniques.name: Animism
techniques.definition: Representation of nonhuman beings, places, objects or forces as agentic, animate or relational participants rather than inert background
techniques.effect: Distributes agency beyond human characters and foregrounds reciprocal relationships between people and the nonhuman world
techniques.example: The river is treated as an ancestor whose memory and choices shape the community
techniques.etymology: From Latin anima, meaning breath, life or soul; the literary term is used here for representations of nonhuman agency and relational presence

techniques.name: Sympathetic Landscape
techniques.definition: Landscape whose physical qualities correspond with a character's or text's emotional condition without necessarily giving nature human feelings
techniques.effect: Makes setting a visual accompaniment to emotion and binds interior state to external scene
techniques.example: After the funeral, bare fields and drained winter light echo the mourner's desolation
techniques.etymology: English critical phrase for landscape made emotionally correspondent with human feeling, described by Jean Hagstrum as a visual accompaniment to emotion

techniques.name: Connotation
techniques.definition: Implied or associated meaning beyond literal definition
techniques.effect: Adds layers of meaning and emotional resonance
techniques.example: Home (warmth, safety) vs. house (neutral)

techniques.name: Denotation
techniques.definition: Literal, dictionary definition of a word
techniques.effect: Establishes precise, objective meaning
techniques.example: Rose: a prickly flowering plant; also romantic symbol

techniques.name: Archaism
techniques.definition: Use of outdated or archaic words
techniques.effect: Creates historical atmosphere or formal tone
techniques.example: Thou, thee, hath, forsooth in Shakespeare

techniques.name: Neologism
techniques.definition: Newly created or recently adopted words
techniques.effect: Signals modernity or innovation
techniques.example: Selfie, cryptocurrency, binge-watch

techniques.name: Colloquialism
techniques.definition: Informal, conversational language
techniques.effect: Creates intimacy and realistic dialogue
techniques.example: Gonna, wanna, ain't in everyday speech

techniques.name: Jargon
techniques.definition: Specialized terminology of a profession or group
techniques.effect: Establishes expertise and insider perspective
techniques.example: Binary, algorithm in programming; tort, statute in law

techniques.name: Slang
techniques.definition: Very informal, often group-specific language
techniques.effect: Creates authenticity and generation/subculture specificity
techniques.example: Lit, flex, salty in contemporary usage

techniques.name: Euphemism
techniques.definition: Mild or indirect term substituted for something harsh
techniques.effect: Softens blow of uncomfortable truth
techniques.example: Passed away instead of died; let go instead of fired
techniques.etymology: Greek euphēmismós: eu- (good) + phḗmē (speech) — 'good speaking'; softening harsh truths

techniques.name: Dysphemism
techniques.definition: Harsh or crude term substituted for neutral one
techniques.effect: Emphasizes negative aspects
techniques.example: Croak instead of die; pig instead of police officer

techniques.name: Register Shift
techniques.definition: Abrupt change from one level of formality to another
techniques.effect: Creates jarring effect or comic contrast
techniques.example: Formal opening followed by slang

techniques.name: Abstract Diction
techniques.definition: Use of general, intangible concepts rather than concrete details
techniques.effect: Emphasizes ideas and themes over specifics
techniques.example: Justice, love, freedom vs. the judge, her embrace, the border

techniques.name: Concrete Diction
techniques.definition: Use of specific, tangible, sensory words
techniques.effect: Creates vivid, immediate imagery and clarity
techniques.example: Oak tree instead of vegetation; bitter cold instead of cold

techniques.name: Latinate Diction
techniques.definition: Use of words derived from Latin or Romance languages
techniques.effect: Creates formal, elevated, or sophisticated tone
techniques.example: Commence, facilitate, ameliorate

techniques.name: Anglo-Saxon Diction
techniques.definition: Use of words from Old English and Germanic roots
techniques.effect: Creates simple, direct, or earthy tone
techniques.example: Begin, help, improve, quick

techniques.name: Loaded Language
techniques.definition: Words chosen for emotional impact beyond denotation
techniques.effect: Manipulates reader's emotions and attitudes
techniques.example: Freedom fighter vs. terrorist; slender vs. skeletal

techniques.name: Nominalization
techniques.definition: Converting a verb or adjective into a noun
techniques.effect: Creates abstraction or formality
techniques.example: Destroy → destruction; happy → happiness

techniques.name: Verbing
techniques.definition: Using a noun as a verb (verbifying)
techniques.effect: Creates energy and directness
techniques.example: Google it, text me, access the database

techniques.name: Idiolect
techniques.definition: The unique, individually distinctive vocabulary, grammar and speech patterns belonging to a specific character or speaker.
techniques.effect: Individualises character through language alone; can signal class, education, culture or psychology without authorial commentary.
techniques.example: Holden Caulfield's repetitive colloquialisms in The Catcher in the Rye, or Shakespeare's gravediggers whose malapropisms mark them as working-class outsiders.
techniques.etymology: Modelled on 'dialect'; from Greek idios (one's own, personal) + lektos (chosen, spoken) from legein (to speak).

techniques.name: Polysemy
techniques.definition: The property of a single word or phrase carrying multiple related or distinct meanings simultaneously within a text.
techniques.effect: Generates deliberate ambiguity and semantic richness; invites multiple readings and rewards the close reader with layered interpretive possibilities.
techniques.example: The word 'heart' operating as organ, seat of emotion and moral courage simultaneously within a single poetic line.
techniques.etymology: From Greek polysemos, meaning 'having many meanings'.

techniques.name: Irony
techniques.definition: Expression of meaning using language that signifies the opposite
techniques.effect: Creates humor, social commentary, or reveals contradiction
techniques.example: Saying 'Oh, great!' when something is terrible
techniques.etymology: Greek eirōneía: eirōn (dissembler) — one who says less than they mean

techniques.name: Sarcasm
techniques.definition: Sharp, bitter taunt or ironic utterance
techniques.effect: Creates mockery and often reveals contempt
techniques.example: Oh, you're so smart—you failed the test
techniques.etymology: Greek sarkazein: 'to tear flesh, gnash teeth' — cutting speech

techniques.name: Cynicism
techniques.definition: Belief that people are motivated by self-interest
techniques.effect: Creates dark, pessimistic tone and detachment
techniques.example: Everyone's got an agenda; no one acts from kindness

techniques.name: Melancholy
techniques.definition: Deep, persistent sadness or pensiveness
techniques.effect: Creates introspective, sorrowful atmosphere
techniques.example: The fading light as day turns to dusk

techniques.name: Wistfulness
techniques.definition: Yearning sadness or nostalgic longing
techniques.effect: Evokes bittersweet remembrance of past
techniques.example: Remembering childhood summers, now forever gone

techniques.name: Reverence
techniques.definition: Deep respect, awe, or veneration
techniques.effect: Creates solemn, dignified, sacred atmosphere
techniques.example: The cathedral's hushed tones and dim light

techniques.name: Detachment
techniques.definition: Emotional distance or objective observation without judgment
techniques.effect: Creates scientific or ironic perspective
techniques.example: He described the disaster with clinical precision

techniques.name: Urgency
techniques.definition: Sense of pressing importance or necessity
techniques.effect: Creates tension and compels reader action
techniques.example: Short sentences, exclamation, present tense in action

techniques.name: Ambivalence
techniques.definition: Simultaneous presence of contradictory feelings
techniques.effect: Creates complexity and internal conflict
techniques.example: Love and hatred for the same person simultaneously

techniques.name: Elegy
techniques.definition: Mournful or contemplative poem; expresses sorrow
techniques.effect: Creates atmosphere of loss and reflection
techniques.example: Formal mourning of the dead or passing of beauty

techniques.name: Sardonic Tone
techniques.definition: Mocking, scornful, with dark humor
techniques.effect: Creates bitter critique with humor
techniques.example: His earnest advice was met with sardonic laughter

techniques.name: Lyric Intensity
techniques.definition: Heightened emotional expression with poetic force
techniques.effect: Creates passionate, deeply personal atmosphere
techniques.example: Overwhelming love, fear, or wonder expressed lyrically

techniques.name: Understatement
techniques.definition: Representing something as less important than it is
techniques.effect: Creates humor or unexpected effect through contrast
techniques.example: A nuclear explosion was 'rather loud'

techniques.name: Hyperbole
techniques.definition: Extreme exaggeration for effect
techniques.effect: Creates humor, emphasis, or surrealism
techniques.example: I've told you a million times; I'm dying of hunger
techniques.etymology: Greek hyperbolḗ: hyper- (over) + bállein (to throw) — 'throwing over'; exaggeration

techniques.name: Alliteration
techniques.definition: Repetition of initial consonant sounds in nearby words
techniques.effect: Creates musicality and emphasizes phrases
techniques.example: The silken, seductive snake slithered softly
techniques.etymology: Latin ad- (to) + littera (letter) — initial sounds repeated in adjacent words

techniques.name: Assonance
techniques.definition: Repetition of vowel sounds within or near each other
techniques.effect: Creates internal harmony and flow
techniques.example: The rain in Spain falls mainly on the plain

techniques.name: Consonance
techniques.definition: Repetition of consonant sounds within or near each other
techniques.effect: Creates texture and rhythmic cohesion
techniques.example: The click and crack of broken sticks

techniques.name: Sibilance
techniques.definition: Repetition of s, z, sh, ch sounds
techniques.effect: Creates hissing, whispered, or menacing effect
techniques.example: The seashell's soft, subtle susurration

techniques.name: Onomatopoeia
techniques.definition: Word that imitates the sound it represents
techniques.effect: Creates immediacy and auditory vividness
techniques.example: Buzz, hiss, crack, bang, meow
techniques.etymology: Greek: ónoma (name) + poieîn (to make) — 'name-making'; sound imitates meaning

techniques.name: Rhyme
techniques.definition: Repetition of terminal sounds in nearby words
techniques.effect: Creates closure, musicality, and predictability
techniques.example: Cat/hat, moon/June in poetry

techniques.name: Internal Rhyme
techniques.definition: Rhyming words within the same line or clause
techniques.effect: Creates compressed musicality and patterning
techniques.example: I held it as I held my breath, as still as stone

techniques.name: Slant Rhyme
techniques.definition: Words with similar but not identical sounds
techniques.effect: Creates modern, imperfect musicality
techniques.example: Home/come, reason/prison

techniques.name: Eye Rhyme
techniques.definition: Words spelled similarly but pronounced differently
techniques.effect: Creates visual rather than auditory rhyme
techniques.example: Love/move, through/though

techniques.name: Cacophony
techniques.definition: Harsh, discordant combination of sounds
techniques.effect: Creates jarring, ugly, or disturbing effect
techniques.example: The grotesque crunch and screech of metal
techniques.etymology: Greek kakophōnía: kakos (bad) + phōnḗ (sound) — harsh, discordant sound

techniques.name: Euphony
techniques.definition: Pleasing, harmonious combination of sounds
techniques.effect: Creates smooth, beautiful, mellifluous effect
techniques.example: Murmuring of innumerable bees; sweet silver sound
techniques.etymology: Greek euphōnía: eu- (good) + phōnḗ (sound) — 'good sound'; pleasing to the ear

techniques.name: Plosive Sounds
techniques.definition: Hard consonants that stop the airflow
techniques.effect: Creates percussive, emphatic effect
techniques.example: Pick and pack the packed picnic basket

techniques.name: Fricative Sounds
techniques.definition: Consonants produced by friction
techniques.effect: Creates hissing, sizzling, or flowing effect
techniques.example: Soft and soothing; fierce and hissing

techniques.name: Sigmatism
techniques.definition: The deliberate or excessive repetition of the 's' sound, often distinguished from general sibilance by its concentration and sustained sinuous quality.
techniques.effect: Creates a hissing, serpentine or whispering acoustic texture; associated with menace, seduction, secrecy or the insidious.
techniques.example: "The slow, sinuous, soundless serpent slid silently across the stones."
techniques.etymology: From Greek sigma (the name of the letter S) + -ismos (suffix denoting practice or condition).

techniques.name: Cross Rhyme
techniques.definition: Rhyme between the end of one line and a word within another line.
techniques.effect: Weaves sound across lines for subtle cohesion.
techniques.example: An end word chiming with a mid-line word in the following line
techniques.etymology: cross from Latin crux, plus rhyme.

techniques.name: Half-Rhyme
techniques.definition: An approximate rhyme in which sounds are similar but not identical, also called para-rhyme.
techniques.effect: Creates dissonance or unease against the resolution of full rhyme.
techniques.example: Wilfred Owen's escaped and scooped
techniques.etymology: half from Old English healf, plus rhyme.

techniques.name: Feminine Rhyme
techniques.definition: A rhyme on a stressed syllable followed by one or more unstressed syllables.
techniques.effect: Softens the close with a falling, gentler echo.
techniques.example: motion and ocean
techniques.etymology: feminine via French from Latin femininus.

techniques.name: Masculine Rhyme
techniques.definition: A rhyme on a single stressed final syllable.
techniques.effect: Produces a firm, decisive chime.
techniques.example: delight and night
techniques.etymology: masculine via French from Latin masculinus.

techniques.name: End Rhyme
techniques.definition: Rhyme occurring at the ends of lines.
techniques.effect: Marks line boundaries and binds the stanza musically.
techniques.example: cat and hat falling at line ends
techniques.etymology: From Old French rime, meaning verse or rhyme.

techniques.name: Rhyme Scheme
techniques.definition: The ordered pattern of rhymes at the ends of lines, conventionally noted with letters.
techniques.effect: Structures the poem's sound and signals its form.
techniques.example: ABAB CDCD in a ballad stanza
techniques.etymology: rhyme from Old French rime; scheme from Greek skhema.

techniques.name: Rhythm
techniques.definition: Pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables in language
techniques.effect: Creates pace and musicality
techniques.example: The iambic heartbeat of a poem's meter

techniques.name: Metre
techniques.definition: Regular pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables
techniques.effect: Creates formal structure and predictable musicality
techniques.example: Iambic pentameter: da-DUM, da-DUM, da-DUM

techniques.name: Iambic Pentameter
techniques.definition: Five iambs per line; common in English poetry
techniques.effect: Creates formal, traditional elegance
techniques.example: Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?

techniques.name: Free Verse
techniques.definition: Poetry without regular meter or rhyme scheme
techniques.effect: Allows natural speech rhythms and flexibility
techniques.example: Much modern and contemporary poetry

techniques.name: Cadence
techniques.definition: The rhythmic rise and fall and modulation of the voice across a line or phrase.
techniques.effect: Shapes the musical contour and emotional pacing of speech.
techniques.example: The falling cadence at the close of a sentence
techniques.etymology: From Latin cadere, meaning to fall, via Italian cadenza.

techniques.name: Iamb
techniques.definition: A metrical foot of one unstressed syllable followed by one stressed syllable.
techniques.effect: Produces the rising rhythm closest to natural English speech.
techniques.example: a-BOVE, be-LOW

techniques.name: Trochee
techniques.definition: A metrical foot of one stressed syllable followed by one unstressed syllable.
techniques.effect: Creates a falling, emphatic or insistent rhythm.
techniques.example: GAR-den, TI-ger

techniques.name: Foot
techniques.definition: The basic metrical unit of a line, made up of a pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables.
techniques.effect: Establishes the rhythmic pulse on which metre is built.
techniques.example: The iamb in a-BOVE

techniques.name: Spondee
techniques.definition: A metrical foot of two stressed syllables.
techniques.effect: Slows the line and adds weight or emphasis.
techniques.example: HEART-BREAK
techniques.etymology: From Greek spondeios, a metre used at libations.

techniques.name: Pyrrhic
techniques.definition: A metrical foot of two unstressed syllables.
techniques.effect: Lightens the line and quickens its movement.
techniques.example: The unstressed pair in to a
techniques.etymology: From Greek pyrrhikhe, a war dance.

techniques.name: Anapaest
techniques.definition: A metrical foot of two unstressed syllables followed by one stressed syllable.
techniques.effect: Produces a brisk, rolling, often comic rhythm.
techniques.example: in-ter-VENE
techniques.etymology: From Greek anapaistos, meaning struck back.

techniques.name: Dactyl
techniques.definition: A metrical foot of one stressed syllable followed by two unstressed syllables.
techniques.effect: Gives a galloping, tumbling momentum.
techniques.example: MER-ri-ly
techniques.etymology: From Greek daktylos, meaning finger.

techniques.name: Syllabic Verse
techniques.definition: Verse whose metre counts the number of syllables per line regardless of stress.
techniques.effect: Imposes shape through count rather than rhythm.
techniques.example: The syllabic poems of Marianne Moore
techniques.etymology: syllabic from Greek syllabe, meaning a syllable.

techniques.name: Accentual Verse
techniques.definition: Verse whose metre counts only the number of stressed syllables per line.
techniques.effect: Roots rhythm in stress rather than syllable count, as in Old English verse.
techniques.example: The four-stress lines of Beowulf
techniques.etymology: accentual from Latin accentus, meaning a tone added to speech.

techniques.name: Sprung Rhythm
techniques.definition: A metre based on counting stressed syllables, with a variable number of unstressed syllables per foot.
techniques.effect: Mimics natural speech with energetic, irregular force.
techniques.example: Gerard Manley Hopkins, The Windhover
techniques.etymology: Coined by Gerard Manley Hopkins from sprung plus rhythm.

techniques.name: Anacrusis
techniques.definition: One or more unstressed syllables at the start of a line before the regular metre begins.
techniques.effect: Provides a rhythmic upbeat into the line.
techniques.example: An introductory unstressed syllable before a trochaic line
techniques.etymology: From Greek anakrousis, meaning a pushing back.

techniques.name: Catalexis
techniques.definition: The omission of one or more unstressed syllables at the end of a line.
techniques.effect: Truncates the metre for abruptness or emphasis.
techniques.example: A catalectic trochaic line dropping its final unstressed beat
techniques.etymology: From Greek katalexis, meaning a stopping.

techniques.name: Tetrameter
techniques.definition: A line of four metrical feet.
techniques.effect: Offers a brisk, song-like measure shorter than the pentameter.
techniques.example: The tetrameter of much hymn and ballad verse
techniques.etymology: From Greek tetra, four, plus metron, measure.

techniques.name: Trimeter
techniques.definition: A line of three metrical feet.
techniques.effect: Creates a short, light or clipped measure.
techniques.example: The three-foot lines alternating in ballad metre
techniques.etymology: From Greek tri, three, plus metron, measure.

techniques.name: Scansion
techniques.definition: The analysis of a line's metrical pattern of stresses and feet.
techniques.effect: Reveals the rhythmic structure underlying the verse.
techniques.example: Marking x / x / across a line to show its iambs
techniques.etymology: From Latin scandere, meaning to climb.

techniques.name: Hexameter (Alexandrine)
techniques.definition: A line of six metrical feet; the iambic hexameter in English is called an alexandrine.
techniques.effect: Lengthens and slows the line for grandeur or closure.
techniques.example: The final line of a Spenserian stanza
techniques.etymology: From Greek hex, six, plus metron; alexandrine from Old French poems on Alexander the Great.

techniques.name: Anaphora
techniques.definition: Repetition of words at the beginning of successive clauses
techniques.effect: Creates emphasis, rhythm, and emotional power
techniques.example: We shall fight, we shall prevail, we shall endure
techniques.etymology: Greek anaphora: ana- (again) + phérein — 'carrying back'; repetition at line starts

techniques.name: Epistrophe
techniques.definition: Repetition of words at the end of successive clauses
techniques.effect: Creates strong closure and reinforcement
techniques.example: When will you learn? When will you see? When will you grow?
techniques.etymology: Greek epistrophḗ: epi- (upon) + strephein (to turn) — 'turning upon' each line end

techniques.name: Symploce
techniques.definition: Combination of anaphora and epistrophe
techniques.effect: Creates complex rhythmic and emphatic patterns
techniques.example: All for one, one for all; each for all, all for each
techniques.etymology: Greek symplokḗ: syn- (together) + plékein (to weave) — weaving anaphora and epistrophe

techniques.name: Epizeuxis
techniques.definition: Repetition of a word with no intervening words
techniques.effect: Creates intense emphasis and immediacy
techniques.example: No, no, NO! Never, never again!
techniques.etymology: Greek: epi- (upon) + zeûgma (yoke) — words yoked directly together

techniques.name: Diacope
techniques.definition: Repetition of words with intervening words
techniques.effect: Creates emphasis with slight variation
techniques.example: Never ever, again and again, far, far away
techniques.etymology: Greek diakopḗ: dia- (through) + koptein (to cut) — word repeated with an interruption

techniques.name: Antanaclasis
techniques.definition: Repetition of a word with different meanings
techniques.effect: Creates wordplay and philosophical complexity
techniques.example: Live to work vs. work to live; light the light

techniques.name: Polyptoton
techniques.definition: Repetition of words with the same root in different forms
techniques.effect: Creates cohesion and explores word relationships
techniques.example: I love the lovingness of those who love life

techniques.name: Leitmotif
techniques.definition: Recurring word, phrase, or pattern representing a theme
techniques.effect: Reinforces central idea and creates textual unity
techniques.example: The repeated word 'home' in stories about belonging
techniques.etymology: German: Leit- (leading) + Motiv (motif) — a recurring 'leading theme'

techniques.name: Refrain
techniques.definition: Line or phrase repeated at intervals throughout a text
techniques.effect: Creates musicality and emphasizes message
techniques.example: The chorus of a song; repeated stanza in poetry

techniques.name: Anadiplosis
techniques.definition: End of one clause repeated at the beginning of the next
techniques.effect: Creates flowing connection between ideas
techniques.example: Strong leaders lead; leaders lead nations

techniques.name: Epanalepsis
techniques.definition: Repetition of word(s) at the beginning and end of a clause
techniques.effect: Creates circular structure and emphasis
techniques.example: Rage against the dying of the light; I came, I saw, I conquered

techniques.name: Conduplicatio
techniques.definition: Repetition of words in close succession for emphasis
techniques.effect: Creates intense emotional and rhythmic power
techniques.example: Cowards die many times before their deaths

techniques.name: Antimetabole
techniques.definition: The repetition of words or phrases in reverse order, often to create a paradoxical or rhetorically forceful structure.
techniques.effect: Produces memorability and rhetorical punch; can reverse, complicate or deepen the logic of a statement.
techniques.example: "Ask not what your country can do for you — ask what you can do for your country." (JFK)
techniques.etymology: From Greek anti (against, opposite) + metabole (change, turning).

techniques.name: Parallelism
techniques.definition: Repetition of grammatical structures in successive phrases
techniques.effect: Creates balance, emphasis, and satisfying rhythm
techniques.example: I came, I saw, I conquered
techniques.etymology: Greek parállēlos: para- (beside) + allēlos (one another) — beside one another

techniques.name: Tricolon
techniques.definition: Series of three parallel items or clauses
techniques.effect: Creates completion and emphasis through triple rhythm
techniques.example: Life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness

techniques.name: Antithesis (Structural)
techniques.definition: Juxtaposition of parallel structures with opposing ideas
techniques.effect: Creates dramatic contrast through syntax
techniques.example: To err is human; to forgive, divine

techniques.name: Chiasmus
techniques.definition: Reversal of grammatical structures in successive phrases
techniques.effect: Creates elegant symmetry and memorable phrasing
techniques.example: Ask not what your country can do for you; ask what you can do for your country
techniques.etymology: Greek khiasmos, from letter chi (X) — crossing structure mirroring the X shape

techniques.name: Isocolon
techniques.definition: Series of grammatically parallel clauses of equal length
techniques.effect: Creates mathematical balance and rhythm
techniques.example: Veni, vidi, vici (I came, I saw, I conquered)

techniques.name: Accumulation
techniques.definition: Piling up of ideas, phrases, or clauses without conjunctions
techniques.effect: Creates overwhelming effect through quantity
techniques.example: The sun, the moon, the stars, the sea, the sky stretched endlessly

techniques.name: Cataloguing
techniques.definition: Listing items in succession
techniques.effect: Creates inventory of details or ideas
techniques.example: Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet

techniques.name: Incremental Repetition
techniques.definition: Repeating a phrase with added elements each time
techniques.effect: Creates building intensity and expansion
techniques.example: I love her, I love her deeply, I love her with all my soul

techniques.name: Amplification
techniques.definition: Expanding on an idea with additional details
techniques.effect: Creates emphasis through elaboration
techniques.example: He was tall—six foot two, broad-shouldered, imposing

techniques.name: Gradatio
techniques.definition: Series of words arranged in ascending order of intensity
techniques.effect: Creates building emotional or logical force
techniques.example: From good to great, from great to magnificent

techniques.name: Auxesis
techniques.definition: The arrangement of words, phrases or clauses in order of increasing importance, intensity or weight, so that each term exceeds the last.
techniques.effect: Builds momentum and rhetorical climax through progressive elevation; the final term carries the greatest emotional and argumentative weight.
techniques.example: "I came with sorrow, with shame, with despair." / "He was a soldier, a leader, a legend."
techniques.etymology: From Greek auxesis, meaning 'growth' or 'increase'.

techniques.name: Congeries
techniques.definition: The heaping up of synonymous or closely related words, phrases or clauses to create cumulative rhetorical force.
techniques.effect: Overwhelms the reader with weight and mass; creates intensity through sheer accumulation rather than through precision or contrast.
techniques.example: "A bloody, barbarous, merciless, inhuman, savage, unrelenting act."
techniques.etymology: From Latin congeries, meaning 'a heap' or 'a pile'.

techniques.name: Simile
techniques.definition: Direct comparison of two unlike things using 'like' or 'as'
techniques.effect: Creates concrete understanding through familiar comparison
techniques.example: The snow was like a blanket covering the earth
techniques.etymology: Latin similis: 'like, resembling' — an explicit comparison

techniques.name: Metaphor
techniques.definition: Implied comparison without 'like' or 'as'
techniques.effect: Suggests deeper connection than simile
techniques.example: Time is money; life is a journey; love is war
techniques.etymology: Greek metaphorá: meta- (across) + phérein (to carry) — 'carrying meaning across'

techniques.name: Extended Metaphor
techniques.definition: Metaphor sustained throughout a work or long passage
techniques.effect: Creates unified symbolic framework
techniques.example: An entire poem where life is a stage with acts

techniques.name: Conceit
techniques.definition: Extended, elaborate metaphor; often intellectual or surprising
techniques.effect: Creates ingenious or witty comparison
techniques.example: Donne comparing lovers' souls to a compass

techniques.name: Personification
techniques.definition: Attributing human qualities to non-human things
techniques.effect: Creates intimacy and emotional connection
techniques.example: The wind whispered secrets; the car refused to start
techniques.etymology: Latin persona (mask) + facere (to make) — 'making a character' of an object

techniques.name: Anthropomorphism
techniques.definition: Giving animals or objects human characteristics
techniques.effect: Creates accessibility and emotional engagement
techniques.example: The brave little toaster; the clever fox outsmarted them

techniques.name: Zoomorphism
techniques.definition: Representing a human being through animal form, traits, behaviour, mental states or imagery
techniques.effect: Recasts human identity through animal comparison and can expose, reinforce or destabilise the boundary between human and animal
techniques.example: He prowled the corridor, shoulders hunched, teeth bared
techniques.etymology: Greek zōon, animal, plus morphē, form; representation through animal form or qualities

techniques.name: Apostrophe
techniques.definition: Directly addressing someone absent or something non-human
techniques.effect: Creates intimacy or dramatic intensity
techniques.example: O death, where is thy sting? Oh, foolish pride!
techniques.etymology: Greek apostrophḗ: apo- (away) + strephein (to turn) — 'turning away' to address the absent

techniques.name: Metonymy
techniques.definition: Substituting the name of something with that of something associated
techniques.effect: Creates conciseness and interesting associations
techniques.example: The White House announced...; Hollywood loves violence
techniques.etymology: Greek metōnymía: meta- (change) + ónyma (name) — 'change of name'

techniques.name: Synecdoche
techniques.definition: Part stands for whole, or whole stands for part
techniques.effect: Creates compressed reference and interesting perspectives
techniques.example: All hands on deck; lend a hand
techniques.etymology: Greek synekdokhḗ: syn- (together) + ekdékhesthai (to receive) — part stands for whole

techniques.name: Allegory
techniques.definition: Extended narrative where characters/events represent abstract concepts
techniques.effect: Creates layered meaning and moral instruction
techniques.example: The Pilgrim's Progress; Animal Farm
techniques.etymology: Greek allēgoría: allos (other) + agoreúein (to speak) — 'speaking otherwise'

techniques.name: Analogy
techniques.definition: Extended comparison highlighting similarities
techniques.effect: Creates understanding of unfamiliar through familiar
techniques.example: How cells work in a body is like workers in a factory

techniques.name: Transferred Epithet
techniques.definition: Applying an adjective to the wrong noun
techniques.effect: Creates surprising image and compressed meaning
techniques.example: A sleepless night (night doesn't sleep); restless sleep

techniques.name: Dead Metaphor
techniques.definition: Metaphor that has become so common it's treated as literal
techniques.effect: Shows how language evolves and metaphors fade
techniques.example: Light a fire; grasp an idea; run a business

techniques.name: Mixed Metaphor
techniques.definition: Combining two or more incompatible metaphors
techniques.effect: Usually considered a flaw; creates confusion
techniques.example: The ball is in your court and the chips are down

techniques.name: Vehicle & Tenor
techniques.definition: Tenor is what's being compared; vehicle is what it's compared to
techniques.effect: Understanding this distinction clarifies metaphor mechanics
techniques.example: In 'love is a rose': love is tenor, rose is vehicle

techniques.name: Hypocatastasis
techniques.definition: A metaphor that is hinted at rather than directly stated
techniques.effect: Creates subtlety and requires reader interpretation
techniques.example: He's such a snake suggests treachery without stating it

techniques.name: Merism
techniques.definition: A figure in which a whole is referred to by naming two contrasting or complementary parts.
techniques.effect: Creates a sense of totality or universality through economical paired opposites; rhetorically satisfying and inclusive.
techniques.example: "Searched high and low." / "Young and old gathered." / "The good and the wicked shall face the same end."
techniques.etymology: From Greek merismos, meaning 'division' or 'partition'.

techniques.name: Adynaton
techniques.definition: A form of hyperbole that asserts an impossibility to emphasise a point.
techniques.effect: Creates comic or emphatic force by anchoring an idea to something that could never occur, amplifying the speaker's conviction through the absurd.
techniques.example: "I'll believe it when pigs fly." / "Sooner would the sea give up her dead."
techniques.etymology: From Greek adynaton, meaning 'impossible'.

techniques.name: Antonomasia
techniques.definition: The substitution of an epithet or title for a proper name, or a proper name for a general idea.
techniques.effect: Compresses character or reputation into a label.
techniques.example: the Bard for Shakespeare
techniques.etymology: From Greek antonomazein, meaning to name differently.

techniques.name: Epithet
techniques.definition: A descriptive word or phrase regularly attached to a name to characterise it.
techniques.effect: Fixes a defining quality, often formulaic in epic.
techniques.example: Homer's rosy-fingered dawn
techniques.etymology: From Greek epitheton, meaning something added.

techniques.name: Kenning
techniques.definition: A compound metaphorical phrase substituted for a noun, as in Old Norse and Old English verse.
techniques.effect: Renames the familiar in vivid, riddling figurative terms.
techniques.example: whale-road for the sea
techniques.etymology: From Old Norse kenning, from kenna, meaning to know or name.

techniques.name: Periphrasis
techniques.definition: The use of an elaborate roundabout phrase instead of a direct word.
techniques.effect: Heightens, dignifies or evades through indirection.
techniques.example: the briny deep for the sea
techniques.etymology: From Greek periphrasis, meaning a roundabout speaking.

techniques.name: Symbol
techniques.definition: Object, person, or action representing something abstract
techniques.effect: Creates layers of meaning beyond literal reference
techniques.example: The ring in LOTR symbolizes power, corruption, and desire
techniques.etymology: Greek sýmbolon: syn- (together) + bállein (to throw) — a token thrown together

techniques.name: Motif
techniques.definition: Recurring pattern, image, or theme throughout a work
techniques.effect: Creates unity and reinforces central concerns
techniques.example: The repeated motif of windows in a story about perspective
techniques.etymology: Latin motivus (moving) via French — a recurring element that 'moves' through a work

techniques.name: Archetype
techniques.definition: Universal symbol or character type recognized across cultures
techniques.effect: Creates instant resonance and deep psychological connection
techniques.example: The Hero, the Shadow, the Wise Mentor

techniques.name: Colour Symbolism
techniques.definition: Colors assigned particular meanings in specific contexts
techniques.effect: Creates atmosphere and communicates symbolically
techniques.example: Red for passion/danger, white for purity, black for evil

techniques.name: Object Symbolism
techniques.definition: Objects representing abstract ideas or themes
techniques.effect: Creates concrete focus for abstract concepts
techniques.example: Mirrors symbolizing self-reflection; cages symbolizing entrapment

techniques.name: Objective Correlative
techniques.definition: A set of objects, a situation or a chain of events arranged to evoke a particular emotion through external sensory facts
techniques.effect: Externalises emotion into concrete circumstance so feeling is evoked rather than directly stated
techniques.example: An untouched cup cooling beside a second empty chair conveys bereavement without naming grief
techniques.etymology: Critical phrase associated with T. S. Eliot's 1919 essay Hamlet and His Problems: external objects, situations or events correlate with and evoke emotion

techniques.name: Animal Symbolism
techniques.definition: Animals carrying particular meanings based on cultural knowledge
techniques.effect: Creates instant association and meaning
techniques.example: Owls = wisdom, foxes = cunning, ravens = death

techniques.name: Mythological Allusion
techniques.definition: Reference to myths or classical stories
techniques.effect: Adds depth by invoking familiar cultural narratives
techniques.example: Calling someone a Trojan horse or referring to Pandora's box

techniques.name: Biblical Allusion
techniques.definition: Reference to biblical stories, characters, or concepts
techniques.effect: Creates moral or spiritual resonance in secular texts
techniques.example: Garden of Eden representing paradise; Judas representing betrayal

techniques.name: Literary Allusion
techniques.definition: Reference to other literary works or characters
techniques.effect: Creates intertextual dialogue and layers of meaning
techniques.example: Referring to Gatsby when describing an eccentric wealthy person

techniques.name: Cultural Allusion
techniques.definition: Reference to cultural events, figures, or artifacts
techniques.effect: Creates contemporary relevance and cultural commentary
techniques.example: References to September 11th or iconic speeches

techniques.name: Emblem
techniques.definition: Visual representation of an abstract quality or concept
techniques.effect: Creates iconic recognition and symbolic power
techniques.example: A crown emblematizes royalty; a skull emblematizes death

techniques.name: Iconography
techniques.definition: System of symbols and their meanings within a text or culture
techniques.effect: Creates recognizable visual language
techniques.example: In medieval art, specific colors and objects carry consistent meanings

techniques.name: Antithesis
techniques.definition: Placing contrasting ideas in parallel grammatical structures
techniques.effect: Creates dramatic opposition and makes both ideas memorable
techniques.example: It was the best of times, it was the worst of times
techniques.etymology: Greek antíthesis: anti- (against) + títhēmi (to place) — 'placing against'

techniques.name: Juxtaposition
techniques.definition: Placing contrasting elements side by side without connectives
techniques.effect: Creates tension and forces comparison
techniques.example: The palace next to the slum; the wedding and the funeral

techniques.name: Oxymoron
techniques.definition: Combining contradictory or incongruous terms
techniques.effect: Creates paradoxical effect and forces reconsideration
techniques.example: Bittersweet, deafening silence, living death
techniques.etymology: Greek oxýmōron: oxys (sharp) + mōros (foolish) — itself an oxymoron

techniques.name: Paradox
techniques.definition: Statement that seems contradictory but may be true
techniques.effect: Creates philosophical tension and requires interpretation
techniques.example: Less is more; to find yourself, you must lose yourself

techniques.name: Foil
techniques.definition: Character, plot point, or idea that contrasts with another
techniques.effect: Highlights qualities through opposition
techniques.example: Enobarbus is a foil to Antony, highlighting different values

techniques.name: Situational Irony
techniques.definition: When reality contradicts expectation in events
techniques.effect: Creates humor, pathos, or philosophical tension
techniques.example: A fire station burning down; a marriage counselor's divorce

techniques.name: Dramatic Irony
techniques.definition: Audience/reader knows something character doesn't
techniques.effect: Creates tension and emotional investment
techniques.example: In Oedipus Rex, we know he's the killer he's seeking

techniques.name: Verbal Irony
techniques.definition: Saying one thing but meaning the opposite
techniques.effect: Creates humor, sarcasm, or critique
techniques.example: Saying 'Oh great!' when something is terrible

techniques.name: Bathos
techniques.definition: Abrupt descent from elevated to trivial or comic
techniques.effect: Creates humor through anticlimax
techniques.example: The hero charges into battle, then trips over a rock
techniques.etymology: Greek bathys: 'deep' — comic descent from elevated to trivial; anticlimax

techniques.name: Anticlimax
techniques.definition: Deflating conclusion that disappoints after buildup
techniques.effect: Creates humor or undermines expectations
techniques.example: After a dramatic opening, the villain monologues pointlessly

techniques.name: Binary Opposition
techniques.definition: Division of concepts into opposing pairs
techniques.effect: Creates fundamental structure for understanding
techniques.example: Nature/Culture, Self/Other, Nature/Nurture

techniques.name: Chiaroscuro
techniques.definition: Contrast of light and dark, often used symbolically
techniques.effect: Creates drama, mood, and symbolic meaning
techniques.example: Dark shadows surrounding a figure in spotlit relief

techniques.name: In Medias Res
techniques.definition: Beginning a narrative in the middle of action
techniques.effect: Creates immediate engagement and requires exposition later
techniques.example: The Odyssey begins with Odysseus already at sea

techniques.name: Flashback (Analepsis)
techniques.definition: Interruption to show earlier events
techniques.effect: Provides context and expands temporal scope
techniques.example: Remembering childhood while in present situation

techniques.name: Flash-Forward (Prolepsis)
techniques.definition: Interruption showing future events
techniques.effect: Creates suspense or foreshadows outcomes
techniques.example: A glimpse of the ending before we reach it

techniques.name: Frame Narrative
techniques.definition: Story within a story; outer frame provides context
techniques.effect: Creates nested narratives and multiple perspectives
techniques.example: Stories told by characters in The Canterbury Tales

techniques.name: Non-Linear Narrative
techniques.definition: Events presented out of chronological order
techniques.effect: Creates complexity and requires active reader engagement
techniques.example: Pulp Fiction jumps between timelines

techniques.name: Circular Narrative
techniques.definition: Ending returns to or echoes the beginning
techniques.effect: Creates completion and philosophical resonance
techniques.example: Story that begins and ends with the same image

techniques.name: Foreshadowing
techniques.definition: Hints of future events or outcomes
techniques.effect: Creates suspense and invites rereading for discovery
techniques.example: A character's comment that becomes prophetic later

techniques.name: Chekhov's Gun
techniques.definition: Principle that introduced elements must be significant later
techniques.effect: Creates causality and meaningful detail
techniques.example: If a gun is mentioned, it must fire by the end

techniques.name: Red Herring
techniques.definition: Misleading clue that diverts attention from truth
techniques.effect: Creates misdirection and surprise
techniques.example: Detective fiction plants false evidence to mislead reader

techniques.name: Cliffhanger
techniques.definition: Abrupt ending on unresolved tension
techniques.effect: Creates urgency to continue reading or watching
techniques.example: End of episode leaves character in danger

techniques.name: Denouement
techniques.definition: Resolution of plot after climax
techniques.effect: Provides closure and reveals consequences
techniques.example: After the climax, events settle and resolve

techniques.name: Rising Action
techniques.definition: Events building toward climax
techniques.effect: Creates tension and emotional investment
techniques.example: Complications and escalations leading to climax

techniques.name: Falling Action
techniques.definition: Events after climax leading to resolution
techniques.effect: Shows consequences and moves toward denouement
techniques.example: After the turning point, events move toward ending

techniques.name: Deus Ex Machina
techniques.definition: Unexpected resolution by intervention of outside force
techniques.effect: Creates artificial resolution
techniques.example: A god appears to solve the otherwise unsolvable problem

techniques.name: Ellipsis (Narrative)
techniques.definition: Omission of events or time periods
techniques.effect: Allows focus on important moments
techniques.example: Skipping over uneventful weeks in a narrative

techniques.name: Subplot
techniques.definition: Secondary plot running parallel to main plot
techniques.effect: Creates complexity and thematic resonance
techniques.example: Love story subplot in an adventure narrative
techniques.etymology: English compound of 'sub' (Latin, under) + 'plot' (a plan or ground plan, of obscure origin).

techniques.name: Parallel Narrative
techniques.definition: Two or more narratives progressing simultaneously
techniques.effect: Creates connection and comparison between stories
techniques.example: Two characters' stories told side by side

techniques.name: Bildungsroman
techniques.definition: A novel tracing the psychological and moral growth of its protagonist from youth to maturity.
techniques.effect: Frames narrative as a process of formation and coming of age.
techniques.example: Charles Dickens, Great Expectations
techniques.etymology: From German Bildung, meaning formation, plus Roman, meaning novel.

techniques.name: Epiphany
techniques.definition: A sudden moment of insight or revelation experienced by a character.
techniques.effect: Crystallises meaning and marks a turning point.
techniques.example: The closing realisation in Joyce's The Dead
techniques.etymology: From Greek epiphaneia, meaning a manifestation or appearance.

techniques.name: Anagnorisis
techniques.definition: Moment of recognition or self-discovery by protagonist
techniques.effect: Creates turning point in understanding
techniques.example: Oedipus discovering he is the cause of the plague

techniques.name: Peripeteia
techniques.definition: Sudden reversal of fortune or circumstances
techniques.effect: Creates dramatic turn in plot
techniques.example: Expected ally reveals they're the villain

techniques.name: Hamartia
techniques.definition: Fatal flaw in protagonist leading to downfall
techniques.effect: Explains tragedy as consequence of character defect
techniques.example: Macbeth's ambition leads to his destruction

techniques.name: Hubris
techniques.definition: Excessive pride or self-confidence that leads a tragic protagonist to defy the gods or moral order.
techniques.effect: Marks the overreach that precipitates downfall, inviting both awe and warning.
techniques.example: Creon's hubris in Sophocles' Antigone brings ruin upon his house.
techniques.etymology: Greek 'hybris' (insolence, outrage, wanton violence).

techniques.name: Nemesis
techniques.definition: The agent or force of retribution that punishes hubris and restores moral balance.
techniques.effect: Delivers inevitable comeuppance, satisfying the audience's sense of justice.
techniques.example: In Greek tragedy, the downfall that follows overweening pride enacts nemesis.
techniques.etymology: Greek 'nemesis' (retribution, indignation), from 'nemein' (to deal out, dispense).

techniques.name: Catharsis
techniques.definition: The purging or purification of the emotions of pity and fear through tragic drama.
techniques.effect: Leaves the audience emotionally cleansed and renewed after vicarious suffering.
techniques.example: Aristotle cites the audience's response to tragedies like Oedipus Rex as cathartic.
techniques.etymology: Greek 'katharsis' (cleansing, purgation), from 'kathairein' (to purify).

techniques.name: Catastrophe
techniques.definition: The final tragic resolution in which the protagonist's fortunes collapse.
techniques.effect: Completes the tragic arc, releasing accumulated tension into downfall and closure.
techniques.example: The deaths that conclude Hamlet form the play's catastrophe.
techniques.etymology: Greek 'katastrophe' (an overturning), from 'kata' (down) + 'strephein' (to turn).

techniques.name: Comic Relief
techniques.definition: A humorous scene or character introduced into a serious work to ease tension.
techniques.effect: Provides momentary release, heightening the surrounding gravity by contrast.
techniques.example: The drunken Porter in Macbeth offers comic relief after Duncan's murder.
techniques.etymology: 'comic' from Greek 'komikos' (of comedy) + 'relief' from Old French 'relever' (to raise).

techniques.name: Dialogism
techniques.definition: The coexistence of multiple competing voices, perspectives or ideologies within a single text, none fully privileged over the others (theorised by Mikhail Bakhtin).
techniques.effect: Creates ideological complexity and resists a single authoritative reading; the text becomes a site of ongoing debate rather than resolved meaning.
techniques.example: The competing voices of characters, narrator and implied author in a polyphonic novel such as Dostoevsky's The Brothers Karamazov.
techniques.etymology: From Greek dialogos (dialogue, conversation) + -ismos; the concept was theorised and named by Mikhail Bakhtin in the 1930s.

techniques.name: Diegesis
techniques.definition: The mode of narration in which events are told or summarised by a narrator, rather than enacted or shown in scene.
techniques.effect: Creates narrative distance; positions the reader as recipient of reported experience rather than direct witness, shaping how much interpretive authority the narrator holds.
techniques.example: "He spent three years at sea, barely surviving." (summary-telling vs. a dramatised scene of those years)
techniques.etymology: From Greek diegesis, meaning 'narration' or 'recounting'.

techniques.name: Dramatic Question
techniques.definition: The central question of suspense that a play raises and the audience waits to see resolved.
techniques.effect: Sustains engagement by focusing anticipation on a single outcome.
techniques.example: "Will Hamlet avenge his father?" is the dramatic question driving the play.
techniques.etymology: 'dramatic' from Greek 'drama' (action) + 'question' from Latin 'quaestio' (a seeking).

techniques.name: Mimesis
techniques.definition: The representation or imitation of the real world in art, central to classical theories of drama.
techniques.effect: Grounds dramatic illusion in recognisable reality, enabling audience belief and emotion.
techniques.example: Aristotle's Poetics defines tragedy as the mimesis of an action that is serious and complete.
techniques.etymology: Greek 'mimesis' (imitation), from 'mimeisthai' (to imitate), from 'mimos' (mime).

techniques.name: Subtext
techniques.definition: The implicit meaning beneath the literal dialogue, conveying unspoken thought or feeling.
techniques.effect: Creates depth and tension by letting characters mean more than they say.
techniques.example: The strained politeness of Chekhov's characters carries grief and longing as subtext.
techniques.etymology: 'sub' (Latin, under) + 'text' from Latin 'textus' (something woven).

techniques.name: Exposition
techniques.definition: The conveying of background information necessary to understand the dramatic situation.
techniques.effect: Orients the audience by establishing setting, character and prior events.
techniques.example: The opening dialogue of many plays delivers exposition about who and where the characters are.
techniques.etymology: Latin 'expositio' (a setting forth), from 'exponere' (to put out, explain).

techniques.name: Syndeton
techniques.definition: Joining phrases or clauses with conjunctions
techniques.effect: Creates connection and accumulation
techniques.example: And we were hungry and tired and afraid

techniques.name: Asyndeton
techniques.definition: Omitting conjunctions between phrases or clauses
techniques.effect: Creates speed, emphasis, or fragmentation
techniques.example: We were hungry, tired, afraid, desperate
techniques.etymology: Greek: a- (without) + syndeton — 'without binding'; conjunctions omitted

techniques.name: Polysyndeton
techniques.definition: Excessive use of conjunctions between phrases or clauses
techniques.effect: Creates rhythmic accumulation or overwhelming effect
techniques.example: And we were hungry and tired and afraid and losing hope
techniques.etymology: Greek: polys (many) + syndeton (bound with 'and') — 'many bindings'

techniques.name: Parataxis
techniques.definition: Placing grammatical units side by side without connectives
techniques.effect: Creates equality and can feel abrupt
techniques.example: I came, I saw, I conquered
techniques.etymology: Greek: para- (beside) + táxis (arrangement) — clauses placed side by side as equals

techniques.name: Hypotaxis
techniques.definition: Using subordinate clauses to show relationships
techniques.effect: Creates hierarchy and complex relationships
techniques.example: When I arrived, since I was tired, although it was late
techniques.etymology: Greek: hypo- (under) + táxis (arrangement) — subordinated, nested syntax

techniques.name: Periodic Sentence
techniques.definition: Main clause postponed until end after subordinate clauses
techniques.effect: Creates suspense and emphasis through delayed resolution
techniques.example: Although we tried, though we failed, still we persevered

techniques.name: Loose Sentence
techniques.definition: Main clause stated first, followed by elaborations
techniques.effect: Creates directness and adds information gradually
techniques.example: We persevered, though we tried, despite our failures

techniques.name: Rhetorical Question
techniques.definition: Question posed not for answer but for effect
techniques.effect: Creates emphasis and engages reader
techniques.example: Who could deny the beauty of the sunset?

techniques.name: Sentence Fragment
techniques.definition: Incomplete sentence used intentionally for effect
techniques.effect: Creates emphasis, mimics speech
techniques.example: Not a complete thought. Just fragments. Sharp. Direct.

techniques.name: Run-On Sentence
techniques.definition: Independent clauses improperly joined
techniques.effect: Can create breathless or manic effect
techniques.example: She ran through the door and down the hall and into his arms

techniques.name: Anastrophe
techniques.definition: Inversion of normal word order
techniques.effect: Creates emphasis or archaic effect
techniques.example: Strong was his conviction; backward he walked
techniques.etymology: Greek anastrophḗ: ana- (back) + strephein (to turn) — inverted word order

techniques.name: Parenthesis
techniques.definition: Insertion of a phrase or clause as interruption
techniques.effect: Allows interjection and creates aside effect
techniques.example: The truth—hard as it is to admit—was obvious

techniques.name: Apposition
techniques.definition: Placement of noun or noun phrase beside another as explanation
techniques.effect: Creates definition through juxtaposition
techniques.example: My brother, the doctor, explained the procedure

techniques.name: Ellipsis (Grammatical)
techniques.definition: Omission of words understood from context
techniques.effect: Creates conciseness and emphasis
techniques.example: Some laughed; others cried

techniques.name: Caesura
techniques.definition: Pause or break in metrical line
techniques.effect: Creates rhythm and allows emphasis in poetry
techniques.example: The day breaks || silence grows

techniques.name: Enjambment
techniques.definition: Line breaks that continue grammatical phrase to next line
techniques.effect: Creates flow across line breaks
techniques.example: The day breaks / silently

techniques.name: End-Stopping
techniques.definition: Grammatical pause coinciding with line ending
techniques.effect: Creates completion and allows rest
techniques.example: The day breaks. / Silence grows.

techniques.name: Brachylogy
techniques.definition: Extreme compression of expression, deliberately omitting words that the reader must infer to complete the meaning.
techniques.effect: Creates intensity, speed and tautness; demands active interpretive participation from the reader and can produce an effect of controlled urgency.
techniques.example: "If possible, come." / "Gone." / "Ready?" / "Three men dead, the rest in flight."
techniques.etymology: From Greek brachylogia, meaning 'brief speech'.

techniques.name: Enallage
techniques.definition: The deliberate substitution of one grammatical form for another — tense, number, person or case — for rhetorical or characterisation effect.
techniques.effect: Can signal dialect, psychological state or defamiliarisation; draws conscious attention to the act of speaking and the social encoding of grammar.
techniques.example: "I seen what you done." (past tense substitution for characterisation) / The royal 'we' substituted for 'I'.
techniques.etymology: From Greek enallage, meaning 'interchange' or 'exchange'.

techniques.name: Anacoluthon
techniques.definition: A grammatical construction in which the expected syntactic sequence is abandoned mid-sentence, leaving it technically incomplete.
techniques.effect: Mimics psychological disruption, emotional overwhelm or a fractured mind; creates authenticity in characterisation.
techniques.example: "If you — but never mind." / "The king — he was very angry."
techniques.etymology: From Greek anakolouthon, meaning 'not following'.

techniques.name: Hysteron Proteron
techniques.definition: A figure in which the natural or temporal order of events or ideas is deliberately inverted.
techniques.effect: Creates urgency, disorientation or dark comedy by presenting result before cause; can suggest emotional priority over logical sequence.
techniques.example: "Put on your shoes and socks." / "I die! I faint! I fail!" (Shelley, Prometheus Unbound)
techniques.etymology: From Greek, literally 'the later earlier'.

techniques.name: Tautology
techniques.definition: The needless repetition of an idea in different words.
techniques.effect: Reinforces a point or exposes empty redundancy.
techniques.example: a free gift
techniques.etymology: From Greek tautologia, meaning saying the same thing.

techniques.name: Pleonasm
techniques.definition: The use of more words than necessary to express a meaning.
techniques.effect: Adds emphasis or, unintentionally, redundancy.
techniques.example: I saw it with my own eyes
techniques.etymology: From Greek pleonasmos, meaning excess.

techniques.name: First-Person Narrator
techniques.definition: Story told from perspective of 'I'
techniques.effect: Creates intimacy and direct reader connection
techniques.example: I walked through the door and found the truth

techniques.name: Second-Person Address
techniques.definition: Story told to 'you'; addresses reader directly
techniques.effect: Creates immediate engagement and implicates reader
techniques.example: You enter the room. You see the body. You freeze.

techniques.name: Third-Person Omniscient
techniques.definition: Narrator knows all thoughts, feelings, and events
techniques.effect: Creates detachment and comprehensive perspective
techniques.example: Traditional omniscient narration in Victorian novels

techniques.name: Third-Person Limited
techniques.definition: Third person but from one character's perspective
techniques.effect: Creates objectivity with limited knowledge
techniques.example: He saw the truth but didn't understand it

techniques.name: Unreliable Narrator
techniques.definition: Narrator whose account cannot be fully trusted
techniques.effect: Creates uncertainty and requires active interpretation
techniques.example: An insane narrator whose perspective is skewed

techniques.name: Stream of Consciousness
techniques.definition: Direct representation of character's mental processes
techniques.effect: Creates immediacy and psychological depth
techniques.example: Molly Bloom's long, unpunctuated internal monologue

techniques.name: Interior Monologue
techniques.definition: Character's unspoken thoughts represented
techniques.effect: Creates access to internal mental life
techniques.example: His thoughts raced: did she know? Could she understand?

techniques.name: Free Indirect Discourse
techniques.definition: Third-person narration with character's voice and perspective
techniques.effect: Creates intimacy without first-person commitment
techniques.example: He wondered if she understood. But how could she?

techniques.name: Epistolary Mode
techniques.definition: Narrative told through letters, emails, or documents
techniques.effect: Creates authenticity and varied perspectives
techniques.example: The novel told entirely through exchanged letters

techniques.name: Dramatic Monologue
techniques.definition: Character speaks directly to listener, revealing self
techniques.effect: Creates character development and psychological insight
techniques.example: Browning's Duke speaking to a visitor

techniques.name: Collective Narrator
techniques.definition: Multiple characters speaking as 'we' or unified voice
techniques.effect: Creates community perspective and shared experience
techniques.example: Townspeople speaking collectively about an event

techniques.name: Naive Narrator
techniques.definition: Narrator lacks understanding of what they describe
techniques.effect: Creates irony as reader understands more than narrator
techniques.example: A child narrator unaware of adults' dark intentions

techniques.name: Ethos
techniques.definition: Appeal to credibility and authority of the speaker
techniques.effect: Establishes trustworthiness and expertise
techniques.example: A doctor speaking about medicine has ethos
techniques.etymology: Greek ēthos: 'character, custom' — credibility-based persuasion

techniques.name: Pathos
techniques.definition: Appeal to emotion and sympathy of the audience
techniques.effect: Engages reader emotionally and motivates response
techniques.example: A story about a child's suffering appeals to pathos
techniques.etymology: Greek páthos: 'suffering, feeling' — appeal that evokes pity or emotion

techniques.name: Logos
techniques.definition: Appeal to logic and reason
techniques.effect: Uses evidence and rational argument to persuade
techniques.example: Statistical evidence presented in logical sequence
techniques.etymology: Greek lógos: 'word, reason' — persuasion through logical argument

techniques.name: Kairos
techniques.definition: Persuasion through timing and cultural moment
techniques.effect: Leverages opportune moment for maximum impact
techniques.example: An ad released during a cultural event it references

techniques.name: Antistrophe
techniques.definition: Rhetorical device turning opponent's words back against them
techniques.effect: Creates clever refutation through reversal
techniques.example: Your own argument proves my point, not yours

techniques.name: Hendiadys
techniques.definition: Expressing a single idea through two words or phrases
techniques.effect: Creates emphasis and semantic richness
techniques.example: Nice and warm; safe and sound

techniques.name: Litotes
techniques.definition: Understatement expressed through negative construction
techniques.effect: Creates ironic emphasis through minimization
techniques.example: That's not bad (meaning it's good); no small matter
techniques.etymology: Greek litótēs: litos (plain, simple) — understatement via double negation

techniques.name: Meiosis
techniques.definition: Deliberate representation of something as less important
techniques.effect: Creates irony and humor through minimization
techniques.example: The Black Death was merely a bit problematic

techniques.name: Apophasis
techniques.definition: Mentioning something by denying it explicitly
techniques.effect: Actually draws attention to what's ostensibly denied
techniques.example: I won't even mention his terrible record

techniques.name: Procatalepsis
techniques.definition: Anticipating and answering objections before they're raised
techniques.effect: Strengthens argument by addressing counterarguments
techniques.example: You might argue costs are prohibitive; however, benefits...

techniques.name: Enthymeme
techniques.definition: Rhetorical syllogism with premise implied rather than stated
techniques.effect: Uses shared understanding to persuade efficiently
techniques.example: All humans are mortal; therefore, Socrates is mortal

techniques.name: Anecdote
techniques.definition: Brief story illustrating a point or providing evidence
techniques.effect: Creates vivid, memorable example and human interest
techniques.example: A personal story told to support a broader claim

techniques.name: Exemplum
techniques.definition: Specific example used to illustrate general principle
techniques.effect: Provides concrete evidence for abstract claim
techniques.example: George Washington's honesty exemplifying integrity

techniques.name: Enumeratio
techniques.definition: Detailed listing of items, points, or arguments
techniques.effect: Creates comprehensive coverage and accumulative effect
techniques.example: Point one, point two, point three...

techniques.name: Hyperbaton
techniques.definition: Inversion of normal word order for rhetorical effect
techniques.effect: Creates emphasis and unusual phrasing
techniques.example: Angry was he; strong the opposition grew

techniques.name: Zeugma
techniques.definition: Word used in two different senses within one phrase
techniques.effect: Creates wit and surprising connection
techniques.example: Lost both her patience and her keys
techniques.etymology: Greek zeûgma: 'yoke' — one word yoking two grammatically different elements

techniques.name: Syllepsis
techniques.definition: Word understood in different ways in successive clauses
techniques.effect: Creates wordplay and surprising connections
techniques.example: Wore an old coat and a smile

techniques.name: Distinctio
techniques.definition: The explicit clarification or distinguishing between multiple possible meanings of a term just used, to prevent ambiguity.
techniques.effect: Controls semantic slippage; signals precision and intellectual rigour in the speaker while anticipating counterargument or misreading.
techniques.example: "I speak of love — not infatuation, not desire, but love in its most deliberate and reasoned form."
techniques.etymology: From Latin distinctio, meaning 'separation' or 'distinction'.

techniques.name: Epanorthosis
techniques.definition: The immediate correction, retraction or sharpening of a word or phrase just used, often to intensify or reframe its meaning.
techniques.effect: Creates an impression of spontaneous rigour and precision; can amplify, qualify or complicate the original statement.
techniques.example: "He was brave — no, reckless." / "A good man, nay, a great one." / "I loved her — I worshipped her."
techniques.etymology: From Greek epanorthosis, meaning 'setting upright again'.

techniques.name: Hypophora
techniques.definition: A figure in which a speaker raises a question and immediately provides the answer, rather than leaving it open.
techniques.effect: Controls the direction of argument; creates a sense of dialogue and guided reasoning while keeping the speaker in command of meaning.
techniques.example: "What should we do? We should act now." / "Was Caesar ambitious? He was." (Shakespeare, Julius Caesar)
techniques.etymology: From Greek hypophora, meaning 'a carrying under' or 'objection answered'.

techniques.name: Aphorism
techniques.definition: A concise statement of a general truth or principle.
techniques.effect: Distils wisdom into quotable, authoritative form.
techniques.example: The unexamined life is not worth living
techniques.etymology: From Greek aphorismos, meaning a definition or distinction.

techniques.name: Epigram
techniques.definition: A brief, pointed and often witty statement.
techniques.effect: Lands a memorable thought with concision and bite.
techniques.example: Oscar Wilde: I can resist everything except temptation
techniques.etymology: From Greek epigramma, meaning an inscription.

techniques.name: Parabasis
techniques.definition: A moment in which the chorus or a character steps fully out of the dramatic fiction to address the audience directly, often on behalf of the playwright.
techniques.effect: Shatters theatrical illusion and implicates the audience in the drama's concerns; creates a meta-theatrical commentary on the events or issues being staged.
techniques.example: In Greek Old Comedy, the parabasis saw the chorus abandon their dramatic role to address Athenian citizens on political and social matters.
techniques.etymology: From Greek parabasis, meaning 'a stepping aside' or 'a going beside'.

techniques.name: Dumb Show
techniques.definition: A passage of mimed action without speech, used to represent or foreshadow events.
techniques.effect: Conveys narrative visually and can foreshadow the main plot in symbolic form.
techniques.example: The dumb show before the play within Hamlet mimes the murder of the king.
techniques.etymology: English compound of 'dumb' (Old English 'dumb', mute) + 'show' (Old English 'sceawian', to look at).

techniques.name: Tableau
techniques.definition: A moment in which actors freeze in a striking arrangement, presenting a silent picture on stage.
techniques.effect: Arrests the action to emphasise a dramatic image or emotional climax.
techniques.example: Nineteenth century melodrama often ended acts on a tableau, holding a frozen pose as the curtain fell.
techniques.etymology: French 'tableau' (picture), diminutive of Old French 'table', from Latin 'tabula' (board).

techniques.name: Dramatis Personae
techniques.definition: The list of characters in a play, conventionally placed at the start of the text.
techniques.effect: Orients the reader and signals relationships, status and roles before the action begins.
techniques.example: The dramatis personae of Hamlet identifies Claudius as "King of Denmark".
techniques.etymology: Latin 'dramatis' (of the drama) + 'personae' (masks, characters), from 'persona' (mask).

techniques.name: Stage Directions
techniques.definition: Instructions in a play's text specifying setting, movement, action or delivery.
techniques.effect: Guides staging and shapes the reader's mental performance, sometimes carrying authorial voice.
techniques.example: The famous direction "Exit, pursued by a bear" in Shakespeare's The Winter's Tale.
techniques.etymology: English compound; 'stage' from Old French 'estage' + 'direction' from Latin 'directio'.

techniques.name: Five Act Structure
techniques.definition: A dramatic structure dividing a play into five acts: exposition, rising action, climax, falling action and catastrophe or resolution.
techniques.effect: Shapes pacing and the rise and fall of tension across a recognisable arc.
techniques.example: Shakespeare's tragedies, such as Macbeth, follow the five act pattern later codified by Freytag.
techniques.etymology: Latin 'actus' (a doing, performance), from 'agere' (to do, drive).

techniques.name: Three Unities
techniques.definition: The neoclassical principles of unity of action, time and place that govern dramatic structure.
techniques.effect: Concentrates the drama for intensity and verisimilitude by limiting its scope and duration.
techniques.example: Racine's Phèdre observes the unities, unfolding in one place within a single day.
techniques.etymology: Latin 'unitas' (oneness), from 'unus' (one); the doctrine was derived from readings of Aristotle's Poetics.

techniques.name: Exodos
techniques.definition: The final scene or departure song after the last stasimon, concluding a Greek tragedy.
techniques.effect: Resolves the action and marks the chorus's exit, delivering closing reflection.
techniques.example: The exodos of Oedipus Rex shows the blinded Oedipus led away from Thebes.
techniques.etymology: Greek 'exodos' (a going out), from 'ex' (out) + 'hodos' (way).

techniques.name: Episode
techniques.definition: A section of spoken dramatic action between choral odes in Greek tragedy.
techniques.effect: Advances the plot and develops character between the chorus's lyric interludes.
techniques.example: The episodes of Euripides' Medea stage Medea's encounters with Creon, Jason and Aegeus.
techniques.etymology: Greek 'epeisodion' (an addition), from 'epi' (upon) + 'eisodos' (entrance).

techniques.name: Stasimon
techniques.definition: A choral ode performed while the chorus stands in the orchestra, between the episodes of a Greek tragedy.
techniques.effect: Reflects on the action, voicing communal judgement and lyric meditation.
techniques.example: The famous "Ode to Man" stasimon in Sophocles' Antigone.
techniques.etymology: Greek 'stasimon (melos)' (stationary song), from 'stasis' (standing).

techniques.name: Parodos
techniques.definition: The first ode sung by the chorus as it enters, in Greek tragedy.
techniques.effect: Introduces the chorus and its perspective, establishing communal mood and context.
techniques.example: The parodos of Aeschylus' Agamemnon recalls the omens at Aulis.
techniques.etymology: Greek 'par(a)' (beside) + 'hodos' (way, path) -> 'parodos', both the side entrance and the song sung on it.

techniques.name: Epilogue
techniques.definition: A concluding section spoken after the main action, offering closure, comment or address to the audience.
techniques.effect: Rounds off the drama, draws a moral or appeals for applause and goodwill.
techniques.example: Prospero's epilogue in Shakespeare's The Tempest asks the audience to set him free with their applause.
techniques.etymology: Greek 'epi' (upon, in addition) + 'logos' (word) -> 'epilogos'.
