techniques.name: Prologue
techniques.definition: An introductory section spoken before the main action, setting context or framing the play.
techniques.effect: Orients the audience, establishes tone and may foreshadow events.
techniques.example: The Chorus's prologue in Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet announces the "star-crossed lovers".
techniques.etymology: Greek 'pro' (before) + 'logos' (word, speech) -> 'prologos'.

techniques.name: Chorus
techniques.definition: A group of performers who comment collectively on the dramatic action, often representing the voice of the community.
techniques.effect: Provides exposition, moral framing and emotional amplification, mediating between stage and audience.
techniques.example: In Sophocles' Antigone, the Theban elders form a chorus that reflects on fate and the limits of human power.
techniques.etymology: Greek 'khoros' (dance, band of dancers) -> Latin 'chorus'.

techniques.name: Stichomythia
techniques.definition: Rapid dialogue in which characters exchange single alternating lines, often in heated argument.
techniques.effect: Heightens tension and pace, dramatising conflict through verbal duelling.
techniques.example: The clipped line-by-line exchanges between Oedipus and Tiresias in Sophocles' Oedipus Rex.
techniques.etymology: Greek 'stikhos' (line, row) + 'mythos' (speech) -> 'stikhomythia'.

techniques.name: Soliloquy
techniques.definition: An extended speech in which a character, alone on stage, voices their inner thoughts aloud for the audience.
techniques.effect: Grants direct access to a character's psychology and moral struggle, building intimacy and dramatic irony.
techniques.example: Hamlet's "To be, or not to be" soliloquy lays bare his contemplation of mortality and inaction.
techniques.etymology: Latin 'solus' (alone) + 'loqui' (to speak) -> Late Latin 'soliloquium', a term coined by Augustine.

techniques.name: Set Speech
techniques.definition: A formal, self-contained speech of some length delivered by a single character within a play.
techniques.effect: Allows sustained rhetoric, argument or emotion, often marking a dramatic high point.
techniques.example: Mark Antony's "Friends, Romans, countrymen" oration in Shakespeare's Julius Caesar.
techniques.etymology: English compound of 'set' (fixed, prepared) + 'speech' (Old English 'spaec').

techniques.name: Aside
techniques.definition: A short remark spoken by a character to the audience or to themselves, conventionally unheard by the other characters on stage.
techniques.effect: Creates intimacy and dramatic irony by giving the audience access to a character's private thoughts while others remain unaware.
techniques.example: In Shakespeare's Hamlet, Hamlet's "A little more than kin, and less than kind" is delivered aside, signalling his contempt for Claudius.
techniques.etymology: From the phrase 'on side' -> Middle English 'asyde'; the theatrical sense is recorded from the early 18th century.

techniques.name: Problem Play
techniques.definition: A drama that stages a contemporary social problem for debate, often without tidy resolution.
techniques.effect: Provokes reflection and discomfort, using the stage as a forum for argument.
techniques.example: Ibsen's A Doll's House confronts marriage and gender roles, leaving its questions open.
techniques.etymology: English compound; 'problem' from Greek 'problema' (something put forward) + 'play' from Old English 'plega'.

techniques.name: Well-Made Play
techniques.definition: A tightly plotted genre built on careful exposition, causal logic and a climactic obligatory scene.
techniques.effect: Delivers satisfying mechanical suspense through neat construction and reversal.
techniques.example: The plays of Eugène Scribe epitomise the well-made play's clockwork plotting.
techniques.etymology: Calque of French 'pièce bien faite' (well-made piece).

techniques.name: Closet Drama
techniques.definition: A play written to be read rather than performed on stage.
techniques.effect: Foregrounds language and idea over spectacle, inviting private, reflective reading.
techniques.example: Milton's Samson Agonistes was conceived as a closet drama.
techniques.etymology: 'closet' from Old French 'closet' (small private room), diminutive of 'clos' (enclosed), from Latin 'clausum'.

techniques.name: Mystery Play
techniques.definition: A medieval religious drama dramatising biblical episodes, often staged in cycles by craft guilds.
techniques.effect: Communicates scripture vividly to a lay audience through communal performance.
techniques.example: The York Mystery Plays dramatise events from Creation to the Last Judgement.
techniques.etymology: From Latin 'ministerium' (service, craft) and 'mysterium' (religious truth), the two senses converging.

techniques.name: Morality Play
techniques.definition: A late medieval allegorical drama in which personified virtues and vices contend for the human soul.
techniques.effect: Instructs morally, dramatising spiritual choice through allegory.
techniques.example: Everyman stages the title figure's reckoning as abstractions like Good Deeds accompany him.
techniques.etymology: Latin 'moralis' (relating to manners or character), from 'mos, moris' (custom).

techniques.name: Masque
techniques.definition: A courtly dramatic entertainment combining poetry, music, dance and elaborate spectacle.
techniques.effect: Celebrates and flatters its noble audience through allegory and visual splendour.
techniques.example: Ben Jonson's masques, designed with Inigo Jones, staged allegories for the Jacobean court.
techniques.etymology: French 'masque' (mask), from Italian 'maschera', of uncertain earlier origin.

techniques.name: Melodrama
techniques.definition: A sensational dramatic genre with heightened emotion, clear moral oppositions and musical underscoring.
techniques.effect: Amplifies feeling and suspense, polarising virtue and villainy for strong audience response.
techniques.example: Nineteenth century stage melodramas pit pure heroines against scheming villains.
techniques.etymology: Greek 'melos' (song, music) + 'drama' (action), via French 'mélodrame'.

techniques.name: Farce
techniques.definition: A broad comic genre relying on improbable situations, physical humour and exaggerated character.
techniques.effect: Provokes laughter through absurdity, mistaken identity and rapid action.
techniques.example: The mistaken identities of Oscar Wilde's The Importance of Being Earnest verge on farce.
techniques.etymology: French 'farce' (stuffing), from Latin 'farcire' (to stuff); comic interludes were "stuffed" into plays.

techniques.name: Tragicomedy
techniques.definition: A genre blending tragic and comic elements, often with a grave threat that resolves happily.
techniques.effect: Complicates tone, mixing pathos with humour to mirror life's ambivalence.
techniques.example: Shakespeare's The Winter's Tale moves from near-tragedy to comic reconciliation.
techniques.etymology: Latin 'tragicocomoedia', a blend coined by Plautus from tragedy and comedy.

techniques.name: Tragedy
techniques.definition: A dramatic genre depicting the downfall of a protagonist through fate, flaw or circumstance.
techniques.effect: Evokes pity and fear, moving the audience toward catharsis.
techniques.example: Sophocles' Oedipus Rex traces the king's ruin through his own investigation.
techniques.etymology: Greek 'tragoidia', perhaps from 'tragos' (goat) + 'oide' (song).

techniques.name: Comedy
techniques.definition: A dramatic genre with a light or satirical tone that typically ends happily, often in marriage or reconciliation.
techniques.effect: Amuses and reassures, resolving conflict and affirming social order.
techniques.example: Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream ends with multiple marriages and harmony restored.
techniques.etymology: Greek 'komoidia', from 'komos' (revel) + 'oide' (song).

techniques.name: Portmanteau
techniques.definition: A word blending the sounds and meanings of two others.
techniques.effect: Coins compact, inventive new terms.
techniques.example: brunch from breakfast and lunch
techniques.etymology: From French portemanteau, a coat-carrier, repurposed by Lewis Carroll.

techniques.name: Spoonerism
techniques.definition: The transposition of initial sounds between two or more words.
techniques.effect: Creates accidental or deliberate comic slips.
techniques.example: a blushing crow for a crushing blow
techniques.etymology: Named after the Reverend William Spooner, noted for such slips.

techniques.name: Malapropism
techniques.definition: The mistaken use of a word in place of a similar-sounding one, to comic effect.
techniques.effect: Produces unintended humour and characterises the speaker.
techniques.example: Mrs Malaprop: a allegory on the banks of the Nile
techniques.etymology: From French mal a propos, meaning inappropriate, via Sheridan's character Mrs Malaprop.

techniques.name: Double Entendre
techniques.definition: A phrase open to two interpretations, one of which is often risque.
techniques.effect: Smuggles a second, usually suggestive, meaning beneath the surface.
techniques.example: A line that reads innocently and bawdily at once
techniques.etymology: From French, meaning double meaning, in an archaic construction.

techniques.name: Pun
techniques.definition: A play on words exploiting multiple meanings or similar sounds, also called paronomasia.
techniques.effect: Generates humour, wit or layered meaning.
techniques.example: Time flies like an arrow; fruit flies like a banana
techniques.etymology: Origin uncertain, perhaps from Italian puntiglio, meaning a fine point.

techniques.name: Allusion
techniques.definition: Indirect reference to another work, person, or event
techniques.effect: Enriches meaning through connection to external reference
techniques.example: Calling an ambitious man an Icarus or Macbeth
techniques.etymology: Latin alludere: ad- (to) + ludere (to play) — 'playing toward' a reference

techniques.name: Quotation
techniques.definition: Direct reproduction of words from another source
techniques.effect: Provides authority or creates deliberate echo
techniques.example: Citing a famous line from another work verbatim

techniques.name: Epigraph
techniques.definition: Quotation placed at beginning of work or section
techniques.effect: Sets tone and provides thematic context
techniques.example: A poem beginning with a relevant Shakespeare quote

techniques.name: Parody
techniques.definition: Humorous imitation of a style or work
techniques.effect: Creates humor through exaggeration of recognizable features
techniques.example: Scary Movie parodying horror film conventions

techniques.name: Pastiche
techniques.definition: Imitation of style, often respectful or admiring
techniques.effect: Honors original while creating new work
techniques.example: A painting in the style of Monet

techniques.name: Homage
techniques.definition: Work created as tribute to another work or artist
techniques.effect: Shows respect and creates intentional echo
techniques.example: A novel dedicated to and influenced by a predecessor

techniques.name: Adaptation
techniques.definition: Rewriting of work in new medium or context
techniques.effect: Translates story to new form while maintaining core
techniques.example: Stage adaptation of a novel; film adaptation of a play

techniques.name: Palimpsest
techniques.definition: Text written over earlier text, or later text reusing earlier
techniques.effect: Creates layered meaning and historical echo
techniques.example: Medieval manuscripts with previous text underneath

techniques.name: Intertextuality (Explicit)
techniques.definition: Clear, named references to other texts
techniques.effect: Deliberately invokes connection reader can identify
techniques.example: Title borrowed from another work
techniques.etymology: Latin inter- (between) + textus (woven) — weaving meaning between texts

techniques.name: Intertextuality (Implicit)
techniques.definition: Subtle echoes and parallels without explicit naming
techniques.effect: Requires reader recognition; creates discovery
techniques.example: Plot structure echoing earlier work without acknowledgment
techniques.etymology: Latin inter- (between) + textus (woven) — weaving meaning between texts

techniques.name: Hypotext / Hypertext
techniques.definition: Hypotext is source text; hypertext is derived text
techniques.effect: Hypotext influences or is transformed by hypertext
techniques.example: Odyssey (hypotext) → Joyce's Ulysses (hypertext)

techniques.name: Breaking the Fourth Wall
techniques.definition: Character or narrator acknowledges audience or fictional nature
techniques.effect: Creates direct connection with reader; disrupts illusion
techniques.example: Character looks at camera; narrator addresses reader directly

techniques.name: Self-Referentiality
techniques.definition: Work referring to itself, its creation, or its status as fiction
techniques.effect: Creates philosophical paradox and self-awareness
techniques.example: Novel discussing its own genre and conventions

techniques.name: Metafiction
techniques.definition: Fiction that reflects on its own nature and conventions
techniques.effect: Creates commentary on narrative and meaning-making
techniques.example: A novel about writing a novel; a film about filmmaking

techniques.name: Postmodern Fragmentation
techniques.definition: Disruptive, fragmented narrative structure
techniques.effect: Challenges coherence and linear meaning
techniques.example: Non-sequiturs, missing pages, disrupted chronology

techniques.name: Unreliable Text
techniques.definition: Text itself seems flawed, inconsistent, or deliberately misleading
techniques.effect: Implicates reader in unreliability and interpretation
techniques.example: Contradictory versions of events; missing pages

techniques.name: Mise en Abyme
techniques.definition: Text containing representation of itself; story within story
techniques.effect: Creates infinite regression and philosophical reflection
techniques.example: A painting depicting the painter painting the painting
techniques.etymology: French: 'placed into the abyss' — infinite mirroring structure within a work

techniques.name: Author Intrusion
techniques.definition: Author's voice breaking into narrative explicitly
techniques.effect: Disrupts fiction and creates author presence
techniques.example: Author commenting on character or plot directly

techniques.name: Narrative Self-Consciousness
techniques.definition: Narrator aware of being in narrative and commenting on it
techniques.effect: Creates philosophical reflection on storytelling
techniques.example: Narrator discussing their own narrative strategies

techniques.name: Epic Theatre
techniques.definition: Brecht's theory of theatre that favours episodic narrative and critical distance over emotional illusion.
techniques.effect: Engages the audience's reason rather than empathy, framing drama as social analysis.
techniques.example: Brecht's The Caucasian Chalk Circle uses a narrator and episodic structure characteristic of epic theatre.
techniques.etymology: Calque of German 'episches Theater'; 'epic' from Greek 'epos' (word, song), 'theatre' from Greek 'theatron'.

techniques.name: Alienation Effect (Verfremdungseffekt)
techniques.definition: Brecht's technique of distancing the audience to prevent emotional immersion and prompt critical thought.
techniques.effect: Keeps spectators aware they are watching a constructed argument, encouraging political reflection.
techniques.example: Brecht's Mother Courage uses placards, songs and direct address to alienate the audience.
techniques.etymology: German 'Verfremdungseffekt', from 'verfremden' (to make strange) + 'Effekt' (effect).

techniques.name: Play within a Play
techniques.definition: A dramatic performance staged inside the main play, watched by its characters.
techniques.effect: Mirrors or comments on the framing action, layering reality and illusion.
techniques.example: "The Mousetrap" staged in Hamlet is a play within a play that traps Claudius's conscience.
techniques.etymology: English descriptive phrase; 'play' from Old English 'plega' (game, sport, performance).

techniques.name: Metatheatre
techniques.definition: Drama that draws attention to its own theatricality, acknowledging that it is a play.
techniques.effect: Breaks illusion to provoke reflection on art, role-playing and reality.
techniques.example: The players and the staged murder in Hamlet make the play self-consciously theatrical.
techniques.etymology: Greek 'meta' (beyond, about) + 'theatron' (place for viewing), from 'theasthai' (to behold).

techniques.name: Metalepsis
techniques.definition: The transgression of narrative levels, as when a narrator enters the story or addresses its making.
techniques.effect: Ruptures the fictional frame to unsettle or amuse.
techniques.example: A character who knows they are being written
techniques.etymology: From Greek metalepsis, meaning a sharing or substitution.
